docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Permio (perms.io) is permissions as a service. It gives you resource-level role-based access control (RBAC): you define permissions and roles, grant them to your users on resource URIs, and ask one question from your code:

May principal alice do document.read on /documents/42?

Manage everything in the dashboard at app.perms.io, and check permissions through the API.

docs.title: Resource-level RBAC
docs.text: Grant access to individual objects, such as /projects/42 or /documents/42/comments/7, not just to whole types.

docs.title: Hierarchical inheritance
docs.text: A grant on /documents applies to /documents/42 and everything beneath it, including resources created later. The _ wildcard segment lets one grant cover a whole level. See Resources and inheritance.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: Grant to a group such as group:editors once, and every member holds the grant. See Groups.

docs.title: Bring your own authentication
docs.text: perms.io only does authorisation. Principals are whatever IDs your app already uses, so it works with any login system.

docs.title: API first
docs.text:
• One REST/JSON, gRPC and gRPC-web API. See the API reference.
  • A TypeScript SDK with check helpers, typed errors, retries and iterators.
  • A dashboard for managing projects, permissions, roles, grants and API keys.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
• Quickstart: from sign-up to a passing check in five minutes.
  • How it works: permissions, roles, principals and grants.
  • API keys: key format, access levels and invalidation.
  • IAM fundamentals: background on access control in general.

docs.title: For AI assistants
docs.text:
If you use a coding assistant or an LLM, point it at these files:

  • llms.txt (https://docs.perms.io/llms.txt): an index of every page on this site, with a one-line description of each.
  • llms-full.txt (https://docs.perms.io/llms-full.txt): the concepts, quickstart, TypeScript SDK and API reference in one Markdown file, to load straight into the model's context.

For example, give your assistant this prompt:

Add Permio permissions to this app using the `permio` npm package. Docs: https://docs.perms.io/llms.txt

Install it with npm install permio. See the TypeScript SDK.

docs.title: Support
docs.text: Questions or problems? Email hello@perms.io.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Permio implements resource-level role-based access control. Your application keeps handling sign-in. perms.io stores who may do what, on which resources, and answers permission checks.

docs.title: Organisations and projects
docs.text:
Your organisation holds your team, billing and projects. A project is a separate space for permissions, roles, grants and API keys. Every organisation starts with a project called default. You might add others, for example to separate environments (staging, production) or products.

Nothing is shared between projects. A check in one project never sees another project's grants.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
A permission is a named action that your code checks, for example:

  • document.read
  • document.write
  • invoice.pay

Names can use letters, digits, ., _ and -, up to 128 characters. A resource.action style works well.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: A role is a named set of permissions, such as viewer = document.read, or editor = document.read and document.write. Granting a role grants all of its permissions.

docs.title: Principals
docs.text:
A principal is whoever you check: usually a user, but it could be a service, a device or anything else. It is identified by a string that you choose, typically the user ID from your auth provider. You don't register principals in advance. A principal appears in perms.io once it has a grant.

API keys are principals too. Each key is granted a role on its own project, which decides what it may call. See API keys.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: A group is a named set of principals in a project, such as editors. Grant to the group's principal ID, group:editors, and every member holds the grant; checks include a principal's groups automatically. See Groups.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: A resource is anything you protect, identified by a URI path such as /documents/42. See Resources and inheritance for the rules.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
A grant gives a principal some permissions and/or roles on one resource URI. A grant applies to that resource and to everything beneath it:

grant viewer to alice on /documents

check alice document.read /documents/42   → passed
check alice document.read /invoices/1     → failed, missing document.read on /invoices/1

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
A check asks: does a principal hold every listed permission on every listed resource? You can check up to 100 resources and 100 permissions in one call.

The answer is passed: true, or passed: false with the missing permissions per resource. A denial is a normal response, not an error. API errors mean the request itself couldn't be carried out, for example because the key is invalid or the input is malformed.

docs.title: Where perms.io fits in
docs.text:
perms.io only does authorisation. It doesn't do authentication.

1. Client ──────────→ Your app: request with a session or token
2. Your app ────────→ Your auth provider: who is this?      → user ID "alice"
3. Your app ────────→ perms.io: may alice do document.read on /documents/42?
4. perms.io ────────→ Your app: passed / missing permissions
5. Your app ────────→ Client: the data, or 403

Your backend calls perms.io with an API key. Keep the key on the server; never ship it to browsers or mobile apps.

docs.title: Managing access
docs.text:
• Dashboard (app.perms.io): create projects, permissions and roles, grant and revoke access on the Principals page, and manage API keys and your team.
  • API: every dashboard action is also an RPC. See the API reference. Writes need an API key with full access, which is on its way.

docs.title: Multi-tenant applications
docs.text:
Put the tenant at the top of every URI and grant tenant admins on the tenant:

/tenants/acme                          ← grant tenant_admin to the Acme admin
/tenants/acme/projects/web-app         ← grant editor to project members
/tenants/acme/projects/web-app/documents/42

A grant under /tenants/acme can never reach /tenants/globex.

docs.title: Per-object sharing
docs.text:
Grant on the exact object to share one document with one user:

grant viewer to bob on /documents/42

docs.title: The same rule at every level
docs.text:
Use _ in a grant to match any single segment, for example to let a moderator manage the comments on every document:

grant comment_moderator to carol on /documents/_/comments

docs.text:
• Follow the Quickstart.
  • Add checks to your app with the TypeScript SDK, including Express and Next.js examples.

docs.title: IAM Fundamentals
docs.text: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a fundamental security framework that controls who can access what resources in your application and what actions they can perform. Understanding IAM concepts is crucial for implementing secure, scalable access control systems.

docs.title: What is IAM?
docs.text: IAM encompasses two core security functions:

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: "Who are you?" - Verifying the identity of users, services, or systems - Login credentials (username/password) - Multi-factor authentication (MFA) - OAuth providers (Google, GitHub, etc.) - API keys and tokens - Biometric verification

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: "What can you do?" - Determining what authenticated entities are allowed to access - Permission checking - Access control policies - Resource-level restrictions - Role-based access control (RBAC)

docs.title: 1. Identity (Principal)
docs.text: An identity (also called a principal) represents an entity that can be authenticated and granted permissions. Identities include:

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Real people with accounts in your system: 

{
  "id": "user_12345",
  "email": "alice@company.com",
  "name": "Alice Johnson",
  "type": "user"
}

docs.title: Service Accounts
docs.text:
Applications or automated systems: 

{
  "id": "service_backup_system",
  "name": "Backup Service",
  "type": "service_account"
}

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
Programmatic access tokens: 

{
  "id": "api_key_67890",
  "name": "Mobile App API Key",
  "type": "api_key"
}

docs.title: Groups/Teams
docs.text:
Collections of users: 

{
  "id": "group_engineering",
  "name": "Engineering Team",
  "members": ["user_12345", "user_67890"],
  "type": "group"
}

docs.title: 2. Resources
docs.text: Resources are the objects, data, or services you want to protect. Everything that requires access control is a resource.

docs.title: Physical Resources
docs.text:
• Servers and infrastructure
  • Database instances
  • Storage systems
  • Network devices

docs.title: Digital Resources
docs.text:
• Files and documents
  • Database records
  • API endpoints
  • Applications and services

docs.title: Logical Resources
docs.text:
• Projects and workspaces
  • Organizations and teams
  • Workflows and processes
  • Configurations and settings

docs.title: Resource Identification
docs.text:
Resources are identified using Resource URIs - hierarchical identifiers that uniquely specify each resource:

/organization/acme
├── /organization/acme/project/web-app
│   ├── /organization/acme/project/web-app/environment/production
│   ├── /organization/acme/project/web-app/environment/staging
│   └── /organization/acme/project/web-app/database/users
├── /organization/acme/project/mobile-app
│   ├── /organization/acme/project/mobile-app/api/v1
│   └── /organization/acme/project/mobile-app/api/v2
└── /organization/acme/billing
    ├── /organization/acme/billing/invoices
    └── /organization/acme/billing/payments

docs.title: 3. Permissions
docs.text: Permissions define specific actions that can be performed on resources. They represent the most granular level of access control.

docs.title: Action-Based Permissions
docs.text:
document.read      - View document content
document.write     - Create or modify documents
document.delete    - Remove documents
document.share     - Share documents with others

docs.title: CRUD Operations
docs.text:
create    - Add new resources
read      - View existing resources
update    - Modify existing resources
delete    - Remove resources

docs.title: Administrative Permissions
docs.text:
admin.users.create    - Create new user accounts
admin.users.suspend   - Suspend user accounts
admin.billing.view    - View billing information
admin.logs.access     - Access system logs

docs.title: Domain-Specific Permissions
docs.text:
deploy.staging      - Deploy to staging environment
deploy.production   - Deploy to production environment
database.backup     - Create database backups
support.tickets     - Access support tickets

docs.title: 4. Roles
docs.text: Roles are collections of permissions that can be assigned as a group. They simplify access management by grouping related permissions together.

docs.title: Predefined Roles
docs.text:
Viewer Role 

{
  "name": "viewer",
  "description": "Read-only access to resources",
  "permissions": [
    "read",
    "list",
    "view"
  ]
}

Editor Role 

{
  "name": "editor", 
  "description": "Can view and modify resources",
  "permissions": [
    "read",
    "write", 
    "update",
    "create"
  ]
}

Admin Role 

{
  "name": "admin",
  "description": "Full control over resources",
  "permissions": [
    "read",
    "write",
    "update", 
    "create",
    "delete",
    "manage",
    "configure"
  ]
}

docs.title: Custom Roles
docs.text:
Create roles specific to your application's needs:

Content Manager 

{
  "name": "content_manager",
  "description": "Manages content creation and publication",
  "permissions": [
    "content.create",
    "content.edit",
    "content.publish",
    "content.review",
    "media.upload"
  ]
}

DevOps Engineer 

{
  "name": "devops_engineer",
  "description": "Manages infrastructure and deployments",
  "permissions": [
    "deploy.staging",
    "deploy.production",
    "infrastructure.configure",
    "monitoring.access",
    "logs.view"
  ]
}

docs.title: 5. Policies
docs.text: Policies define the rules that govern access control. They specify which principals can perform which actions on which resources under what conditions.

docs.title: Basic Policy Structure
docs.text:
{
  "principal": "user_alice",
  "resource": "/project/web-app/database/users",
  "permissions": ["read", "write"],
  "effect": "allow"
}

docs.title: Conditional Policies
docs.text:
{
  "principal": "group_developers",
  "resource": "/project/*/environment/staging",
  "permissions": ["deploy"],
  "effect": "allow",
  "conditions": {
    "time_of_day": "09:00-17:00",
    "source_ip": "10.0.0.0/8"
  }
}

In Permio

Permio uses grants rather than policy documents: a principal, a resource URI, and permissions and/or roles. It has no deny effect and no conditions such as time of day or source IP. If you need conditions, apply them in your application before or after the permission check.

docs.title: 1. Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
docs.text:
Resource owners control access to their resources:

  • User-controlled: Individual users set permissions
  • Flexible: Easy to share and delegate access
  • Scalability issues: Difficult to manage at scale
  • Security risks: Users may grant excessive permissions

Example: File system permissions where file owners can set read/write permissions for other users.

docs.title: 2. Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
docs.text:
System-wide policies control access:

  • Centrally controlled: Administrators set all permissions
  • Security focused: Strong security guarantees
  • Inflexible: Difficult to adapt to changing needs
  • Complex: Requires detailed security classifications

Example: Military security systems with Top Secret, Secret, and Confidential classifications.

docs.title: 3. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
docs.text:
Access based on user roles within the organization:

  • Role-centric: Permissions assigned to roles, not individuals
  • Scalable: Easy to manage large numbers of users
  • Organizational alignment: Reflects real-world job functions
  • Standard approach: Widely adopted in business applications

docs.title: RBAC Components
docs.text:
Users ──→ Roles ──→ Permissions ──→ Objects/Resources
  │                                          
  └─────→ Sessions ──→ Roles

Users → assigned to → Roles → granted → Permissions → on → Resources

docs.title: RBAC Example
docs.text:
Alice (User) → Editor Role → [read, write, publish] → /blog/posts/*
Bob (User) → Viewer Role → [read] → /blog/posts/*
Carol (User) → Admin Role → [read, write, delete, manage] → /blog/*

docs.title: 4. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
docs.text:
Dynamic access based on attributes:

  • Context-aware: Considers user, resource, and environmental attributes
  • Fine-grained: Very precise access control
  • Complex: Requires sophisticated policy engines
  • Flexible: Adapts to complex business rules

docs.title: ABAC Example
docs.text:
{
  "policy": "Allow access if user is manager AND resource is in their department AND current time is business hours",
  "user_attributes": {
    "role": "manager",
    "department": "engineering",
    "clearance_level": "3"
  },
  "resource_attributes": {
    "department": "engineering", 
    "classification": "internal",
    "data_type": "source_code"
  },
  "environment_attributes": {
    "time": "14:30",
    "day_of_week": "Tuesday",
    "location": "office_network"
  }
}

docs.title: Hierarchical Resources
docs.text:
Resources often exist in hierarchical relationships where permissions granted at higher levels automatically apply to lower levels:

/organization/acme                 ← Admin permissions here
├── /organization/acme/project/web ← apply to all projects
│   ├── /environment/staging       ← and all environments
│   └── /environment/production    ← within those projects
└── /organization/acme/project/api
    ├── /environment/staging
    └── /environment/production

docs.title: Inheritance Rules
docs.text:
Systems differ in how they combine inherited and explicit grants. Some support explicit denies or "closest parent wins" rules.

In Permio

Grants are purely additive: there are no deny rules. A principal holds a permission on a resource if any grant on that resource or on one of its ancestors gives it. See Resources and inheritance.

docs.title: Inheritance Example
docs.text:
Given these permission assignments: 

[
  {
    "principal": "alice",
    "resource": "/organization/acme",
    "permissions": ["read"]
  },
  {
    "principal": "alice", 
    "resource": "/organization/acme/project/web",
    "permissions": ["write"]
  },
]

Alice's effective permissions: - /organization/acme and everything beneath it: read - /organization/acme/project/web and everything beneath it: read + write (inherited + explicit)

docs.title: 1. Principle of Least Privilege
docs.text:
Grant the minimum permissions necessary for users to perform their job functions:

// Good: Specific permissions
{
  "role": "content_editor",
  "permissions": [
    "articles.create",
    "articles.edit", 
    "articles.publish",
    "media.upload"
  ]
}

// Avoid: Overly broad permissions
{
  "role": "content_editor", 
  "permissions": [
    "admin.*",
    "system.*"
  ]
}

docs.title: 2. Role-Based Organization
docs.text:
Design roles that mirror your organization structure:

{
  "engineering_roles": [
    "software_engineer",
    "senior_engineer", 
    "engineering_manager",
    "principal_engineer"
  ],
  "product_roles": [
    "product_manager",
    "product_owner",
    "product_analyst"
  ],
  "operations_roles": [
    "devops_engineer",
    "site_reliability_engineer",
    "system_administrator"
  ]
}

docs.title: 3. Resource Hierarchy Design
docs.text:
Create logical resource hierarchies that support inheritance:

# Good: Logical hierarchy
/company/departments/engineering/teams/platform/projects/auth-service

# Avoid: Flat structure
/auth-service-engineering-platform-team

docs.title: 4. Regular Access Reviews
docs.text:
Implement periodic reviews of permissions:

  • Quarterly access reviews: Review all role assignments
  • Project completion: Remove project-specific access
  • Role changes: Update permissions when people change roles
  • Offboarding: Immediately revoke all access when people leave

docs.title: 5. Audit and Logging
docs.text:
Track all access control decisions:

{
  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "principal": "alice@company.com",
  "resource": "/project/web-app/database/users",
  "action": "read",
  "result": "allowed",
  "reason": "role:database_reader"
}

docs.title: 6. Separation of Duties
docs.text:
Prevent conflicts of interest by separating incompatible functions:

// Finance roles - separate creation from approval
{
  "expense_creator": ["expense.create", "expense.submit"],
  "expense_approver": ["expense.approve", "expense.reject"],
  "expense_payer": ["payment.create", "payment.execute"]
}

// Development roles - separate development from production  
{
  "developer": ["code.write", "deploy.staging"],
  "release_manager": ["deploy.production", "rollback.production"]
}

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Effective IAM is critical for application security and requires careful planning and implementation. Key takeaways:

  • Start simple: Begin with basic RBAC and expand as needed
  • Think hierarchically: Design resource structures that support inheritance
  • Follow best practices: Implement least privilege, separation of duties, and regular reviews
  • Monitor continuously: Track access patterns and audit permissions regularly
  • Choose the right tools: Select IAM solutions that fit your architecture and scale

Ready to try it? The Quickstart takes you from sign-up to a working permission check.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This guide takes you from a new account to a passing permission check in about five minutes. You'll use the dashboard to set things up, then make the check from code.

docs.title: 1. Sign up
docs.text:
Go to app.perms.io and click Sign up. You can sign up with email and password or with Google.

Next, name your organisation and click Create organisation. The organisation holds your projects, API keys, billing and team.

docs.title: 2. Use the default project
docs.text:
A project called default is created with your organisation, and the dashboard selects it for you. Permissions, roles, grants and API keys all belong to a project. You can switch projects, or create more, from the project switcher at the top of the dashboard.

This guide uses default throughout.

docs.title: 3. Create a permission and a role
docs.text:
A permission is an action your code checks, such as document.read. A role is a named set of permissions.

  1. Open Permissions and click Create Permission. Enter the name document.read, optionally add a description, and click Create permission.
  2. Open Roles and click Create New Role. Enter the name viewer, tick document.read under Permissions, and click Create role.

Tip

A permission's name is the string your code checks, and it can't be renamed later. A resource.action style such as document.read works well.

docs.title: 4. Grant the role to a principal on a resource
docs.text:
A principal is whoever you are checking: usually one of your users, identified by the ID your app already uses. perms.io doesn't need to know about the principal in advance.

  1. Open Principals and click Grant Access.
  2. Fill in:
    • Principal ID: alice
    • Resource URI: /documents
    • Roles: viewer
  3. Click Grant access.

Alice can now read /documents and everything beneath it.

docs.title: 5. Create an API key
docs.text:
1. Open API Keys and click Create New Key.
  2. Name it, for example quickstart, and click Create key.
  3. Copy the key. It is only shown once.

Keys look like perms_ followed by 38 letters and digits. Keep the key on your server. See API keys for details.

docs.title: 6. Make a check
docs.text:
Ask whether alice may read document 42:

API hosts

Environment Base URL Production https://api.perms.io Development https://dev-api.perms.io

The examples on this site read the host from a PERMIO_API shell variable, so you only need to change it in one place:

export PERMIO_API=https://api.perms.io
export PERMIO_API_KEY=perms_...   # your API key
TypeScriptcURL 
npm install permio

import { Permio, resource } from "permio";

const permio = new Permio({
  apiKey: process.env.PERMIO_API_KEY!,
  project: "default",
});

const allowed = await permio.check({
  principal: "alice",
  resource: resource("documents", 42), // "/documents/42"
  permission: "document.read",
});

console.log(allowed); // true

curl -X POST "$PERMIO_API/permissions-service/v1/permissions/check" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PERMIO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "project_name": "default",
    "principal_id": "alice",
    "resource_uris": ["/documents/42"],
    "permissions": ["document.read"]
  }'

{"passed": true}

The check passes even though you never granted anything on /documents/42. The grant on /documents is inherited by every resource beneath it.

docs.title: A denied check
docs.text:
Now check a resource outside /documents:

TypeScriptcURL 
const result = await permio.checkDetailed({
  principal: "alice",
  resource: "/invoices/1",
  permission: "document.read",
});

console.log(result);
// { allowed: false, missing: [{ resource: "/invoices/1", permissions: ["document.read"] }] }

curl -X POST "$PERMIO_API/permissions-service/v1/permissions/check" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PERMIO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "project_name": "default",
    "principal_id": "alice",
    "resource_uris": ["/invoices/1"],
    "permissions": ["document.read"]
  }'

{"missingPermissions": [{"resourceUri": "/invoices/1", "missingPermissions": ["document.read"]}]}

JSON responses use camelCase field names and leave out fields with default values, so "passed": false is not printed.

A denial is a normal answer, not an error. You get a successful response with passed false and a list of what is missing. Errors are kept for problems with the request itself: a bad key, malformed input or a key that isn't allowed to check. See Errors.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Resources and inheritance: design your resource URIs, and use the _ wildcard.
  • Groups: grant to a team once instead of to each user.
  • TypeScript SDK: assert, checkAny, error handling, and Express and Next.js examples.
  • API reference: every endpoint, for cURL, gRPC and the generated clients.

docs.title: API overview
docs.text:
The perms.io API has two services:

Service Proto What it does Permissions permio.permissions.v1.PermissionsService Permissions, roles, grants and checks. This is the service your application calls. Organisations permio.organisation.v1.OrganisationService Organisations, projects, API keys and team members. Mostly used by the dashboard.

Both are defined in Permio's protobuf definitions. The same host serves them as REST/JSON, gRPC and gRPC-web.

API hosts

Environment Base URL Production https://api.perms.io Development https://dev-api.perms.io

The examples on this site read the host from a PERMIO_API shell variable, so you only need to change it in one place:

export PERMIO_API=https://api.perms.io
export PERMIO_API_KEY=perms_...   # your API key

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
Protocol How to call it REST/JSON The HTTP method and path listed for each RPC in this reference, for example POST $PERMIO_API/permissions-service/v1/permissions/check. Request bodies accept the proto field names (project_name). Responses use camelCase JSON names (missingPermissions) and leave out fields that have default values. gRPC Connect to the host on port 443 with TLS, for example api.perms.io:443, and send the key as authorization metadata. gRPC-web The protocol the TypeScript SDK uses. It works from servers, edge runtimes and browsers.

For GET and DELETE requests over REST, fields that aren't in the path go in the query string. Nested fields use dot notation, for example ?project_name=default&pagination.limit=50.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every request needs an API key, sent as a bearer token:

Authorization: Bearer perms_...

Keys are 44 characters long: perms_, 32 random base62 characters and a 6-character checksum. A key is shown once, when you create it in the dashboard. Only a hash of it is stored, and you can invalidate it at any time. Older JWT API keys are still accepted.

A key acts within its own project. Your organisation is worked out from the key, so permission requests don't include an organisation ID. A key gets its own grants on its project: by default check access, which allows Check, the access queries and the read-only calls. See Access levels.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A denied check is not an error. Check returns success with passed: false and a list of missing_permissions. Errors mean that the request itself could not be carried out:

gRPC status HTTP Meaning INVALID_ARGUMENT (3) 400 Malformed input: an invalid resource URI, an empty permissions list, a bad project name, more than 100 items in a check, and so on. UNAUTHENTICATED (16) 401 The API key is missing, malformed, unknown or invalidated. PERMISSION_DENIED (7) 403 The API key isn't allowed to make this call. For example, a key without permission.check calling Check, or a check-only key creating a role. The message lists what is missing. NOT_FOUND (5) 404 The permission, role, group or other entity doesn't exist. Also returned when a group:<slug> principal names a group that doesn't exist. ALREADY_EXISTS (6) 409 A group with this name already exists in the project. INTERNAL (13) 500 Something went wrong on our side. UNAVAILABLE (14) 503 The service is temporarily unavailable. Safe to retry for reads.

Over REST, the error body carries the gRPC code and a message:

{"code": 16, "message": "invalid api key"}

Over gRPC and gRPC-web, the code arrives as grpc-status and the text as grpc-message.

docs.title: Organisations & Projects
docs.text:
permio.organisation.v1.OrganisationService manages organisations, projects, API keys and team members. The dashboard is built on it, and it's the easiest way to do all of this.

Mostly for the dashboard

These calls check organisation-level permissions such as project.create or apiKeys.list. Dashboard users get these through their role in the organisation. An API key's project grants don't include them, so most calls on this page return PERMISSION_DENIED for an API key.

API hosts

Environment Base URL Production https://api.perms.io Development https://dev-api.perms.io

The examples on this site read the host from a PERMIO_API shell variable, so you only need to change it in one place:

export PERMIO_API=https://api.perms.io
export PERMIO_API_KEY=perms_...   # your API key

docs.text:

Permissions & Roles
docs.text:
permio.permissions.v1.PermissionsService stores permissions, roles and grants, and answers checks. Every request names a project_name. Your organisation comes from the API key.

API hosts

Environment Base URL Production https://api.perms.io Development https://dev-api.perms.io

The examples on this site read the host from a PERMIO_API shell variable, so you only need to change it in one place:

export PERMIO_API=https://api.perms.io
export PERMIO_API_KEY=perms_...   # your API key

In the tables below, Key access is the API key access level needed to make the call. Check is the default for new keys, and Full is the level that also allows writes.

docs.text: Field Rule project_name 1–32 characters: lowercase letters, digits and -. Permission name 1–128 characters: a-z A-Z 0-9 . _ -. Role name 1–128 characters, no control characters. Role id 1–128 characters: a-z A-Z 0-9 . _ -. Group name 1–64 characters: lowercase letters, digits and -. Its principal ID is group:<name>. Principal IDs Any non-empty string. IDs starting with group: are reserved for groups: such an ID must name a group that exists in the project, or the call fails with NOT_FOUND (INVALID_ARGUMENT if it isn't a valid group name). Revoking is the exception. Resource URIs See Resources and inheritance.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
POST /permissions-service/v1/permissions/check

Checks whether a principal holds every listed permission on every listed resource. Grants on ancestors of a resource count, and so do grants to the groups the principal is a member of. See how a check is decided. To get one answer per resource, use BatchCheck.

Request (CheckPermissionRequest)

Field Type Description project_name string Required. Project to check in. principal_id string Required. The principal being checked. resource_uris string[] Required. 1–100 unique resource URIs. permissions string[] Required. 1–100 unique permission names.

Response (CheckPermissionResponse)

Field Type Description passed bool true if every permission is held on every resource. missing_permissions MissingPermissions[] For each resource that failed: resource_uri and the missing_permissions not held there.

A failed check is a successful response with passed: false. PERMISSION_DENIED means the API key lacks permission.check on the resources or on the principal, not that the principal was denied.

TypeScriptcURL 
const { allowed, missing } = await permio.checkDetailed({
  principal: "alice",
  resources: ["/documents/42", "/invoices/1"],
  permission: "document.read",
});

curl -X POST "$PERMIO_API/permissions-service/v1/permissions/check" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PERMIO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "project_name": "default",
    "principal_id": "alice",
    "resource_uris": ["/documents/42", "/invoices/1"],
    "permissions": ["document.read"]
  }'

{"missingPermissions": [{"resourceUri": "/invoices/1", "missingPermissions": ["document.read"]}]}

docs.title: BatchCheck
docs.text:
POST /permissions-service/v1/permissions/check/batch

Checks a principal's permissions on each resource separately and returns one result per resource, in request order. It is evaluated exactly like Check: inheritance, stored _ wildcards, roles and the principal's groups all count, and it fails closed. A resource is allowed only if the principal holds every requested permission on it.

Needs: the same as Check: permission.check on every resource and on the principal.

Request (BatchCheckRequest)

Field Type Description project_name string Required. Project to check in. principal_id string Required. The principal being checked. resource_uris string[] Required. 1–100 unique resource URIs, with the same rules as Check. permissions string[] Required. 1–100 unique permission names.

Response (BatchCheckResponse)

Field Type Description results BatchCheckResult[] One per requested resource, in request order.

BatchCheckResult

Field Type Description resource_uri string The resource. allowed bool true if the principal holds every requested permission on it. missing_permissions string[] The requested permissions not held on it, in request order.

Errors: INVALID_ARGUMENT for a malformed request; PERMISSION_DENIED if the API key lacks permission.check; NOT_FOUND if principal_id is group:<slug> and that group doesn't exist.

TypeScriptcURLGoPythonRust 
const allowed = await permio.batchCheck({
  principal: "alice",
  resources: ["/documents/42", "/invoices/1"],
  permission: "document.read",
});
allowed.get("/documents/42"); // true

Available from SDK 0.2.0. batchCheckDetailed returns the missing permissions too. See Batch checks.

curl -X POST "$PERMIO_API/permissions-service/v1/permissions/check/batch" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PERMIO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "project_name": "default",
    "principal_id": "alice",
    "resource_uris": ["/documents/42", "/invoices/1"],
    "permissions": ["document.read"]
  }'

{"results": [
  {"resourceUri": "/documents/42", "allowed": true},
  {"resourceUri": "/invoices/1", "missingPermissions": ["document.read"]}
]}

res, err := client.BatchCheck(ctx, &permissionsv1.BatchCheckRequest{
    ProjectName:  "default",
    PrincipalId:  "alice",
    ResourceUris: []string{"/documents/42", "/invoices/1"},
    Permissions:  []string{"document.read"},
})
// handle err
for _, r := range res.GetResults() {
    fmt.Println(r.GetResourceUri(), r.GetAllowed())
}

res = client.BatchCheck(
    permissions_pb2.BatchCheckRequest(
        project_name="default",
        principal_id="alice",
        resource_uris=["/documents/42", "/invoices/1"],
        permissions=["document.read"],
    ),
    metadata=[("authorization", f"Bearer {api_key}")],
)
for r in res.results:
    print(r.resource_uri, r.allowed)

use permio_rust::permissions::v1::BatchCheckRequest;

let res = client
    .batch_check(BatchCheckRequest {
        project_name: "default".into(),
        principal_id: "alice".into(),
        resource_uris: vec!["/documents/42".into(), "/invoices/1".into()],
        permissions: vec!["document.read".into()],
    })
    .await?
    .into_inner();
for r in res.results {
    println!("{} {}", r.resource_uri, r.allowed);
}

The Go, Python and Rust examples use a client set up as in Clients.

docs.title: GrantUserPermissionsAndRolesOnResource
docs.text:
POST /permissions-service/v1/permissions/assign

Grants permissions and/or roles to a principal on a resource. Grants are additive: existing grants are kept. The grant also applies to every resource beneath resource_uri. Unknown permissions or roles are rejected with INVALID_ARGUMENT.

To grant to a group, set user_id to group:<slug>. The group must exist in the project, or the call fails with NOT_FOUND. Every member of the group then holds the grant. Grants to groups don't count towards your unique principals.

Field Type Description project_name string Required. user_id string Required. The principal ID, the same value you pass as principal_id to Check. resource_uri string Required. permissions string[] Permission names. roles string[] Role IDs. TypeScriptcURL 
await permio.permissions.grantUserPermissionsAndRolesOnResource({
  projectName: "default",
  userId: "alice",
  resourceUri: "/documents",
  roles: [roleId],
});

curl -X POST "$PERMIO_API/permissions-service/v1/permissions/assign" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PERMIO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"project_name": "default", "user_id": "alice", "resource_uri": "/documents", "roles": ["ROLE_ID"]}'

  projectName: "default",
  userId: "alice",
  resourceUri: "/documents",
  roles: [roleId],

  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PERMIO_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"project_name": "default", "user_id": "alice", "resource_uri": "/documents", "roles": ["ROLE_ID"]}'
